source.title: Mitigating Memorization of Noisy Labels via Regularization between Representations
source.authors: Hao Cheng; Zhaowei Zhu; Xing Sun; Yang Liu

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendix; no obvious truncation affects the reported findings.
record.tranche_reason: The paper directly analyzes and experimentally examines memorization of corrupted labels. It refines the broad memorization claim by showing effects depend on noise type, noise rate, model capacity, encoder treatment, and regularization. Its experiments do not test the original claim's fully random labels or unstructured inputs.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's reported experiments comparing training/test behavior under label noise and regularization, plus the down-sampling result. Mentioned prior-work findings, including random-label fitting and clean-first learning attributed to other studies, are not rows. Figure-only learning-dynamics results are included only where the accompanying text describes the result.
record.test_reason: The study provides its own training/test curves under symmetric label noise and test-accuracy sweeps across corruption rates, bearing on V4. Most extracted rows instead compare mitigation methods and cannot establish the listed claims. Neither better mitigation nor incomplete measurement warrants the record's T5 verdict.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate. More precisely, the authors derive generalization-error bounds relating noise rate, sample size, and capacity, analyze the tradeoff between fixed and unfixed encoders, and propose representation regularization to mitigate noisy-label overfitting. A smaller bound is not proof that a lower-capacity model always performs better.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic and real-world label-noise experiments, compares fixed versus unfixed encoders, and adds a self-supervised representation regularizer. It does not reproduce the original random-label intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with symmetric noise rate, noise type (symmetric, asymmetric, instance-dependent), dataset, initialization, and whether the encoder is fixed or unfixed. The representation regularizer's effect also varies by robust loss and reported epoch metric.

fits_no_version.finding: Freezing pretrained encoders improves stability and favors high symmetric noise; allowing encoder updates favors low noise or biased noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The preferred encoder treatment depends on noise level and noise structure.

fits_no_version.finding: Representation regularization generally improves noisy-label test performance and reduces late-training deterioration, with exceptions across losses and metrics.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Matching supervised-output relations to self-supervised feature relations can mitigate noisy-label overfitting.

fits_no_version.finding: Down-sampling improves performance under instance-dependent noise; the analysis attributes this to reducing noise-rate imbalance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Balancing observed labels can reduce noise-rate imbalance and improve noisy-label learning under specified conditions.

record.problems: No completely random-label experiment, shuffled-input experiment, or explicit regularizer ablation matching V5 is reported. Much of the learning-dynamics evidence appears only in figures without numeric values. Experiments focus on selected noise regimes and datasets; no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results were left out. Results cited from other work, including clean-first learning attributed to Arpit et al. (2017), are excluded as prior-work claims.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training error and chance test performance on completely random labels with unchanged architecture and hyperparameters. The DogCat sweep reaches the random-label threshold, but training fit is not reported.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence slowing as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit throughout the full corruption range, the fully random endpoint for standard end-to-end training, and direct separation of signal learning from noise memorization. Best-epoch test sweeps do not establish these parts.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and true-label generalization after removing them.
Separate measurements of clean-label and noisy-label learning order. The clean-first statement cites Arpit et al.; aggregate test curves do not independently establish that order.

missing.what: Figure 1 reports the study's training and test accuracies on CIFAR10 at symmetric noise rates 0.4 and 0.6. The accompanying text describes increasing training accuracy with late-stage test deterioration. Add these curves separately; exact endpoints and perfect training fit cannot be recovered from the supplied text.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's limits_scope verdicts: changing mitigation performance does not contradict V4, and unmeasured training fit belongs under untested. Symmetric noise here flips labels uniformly to other classes, so complete label independence occurs at (K−1)/K, rather than flip probability 1. The supplied manuscript does not substantiate the record's ICLR 2021 publication claim.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment assigns completely random labels to the training set or tests chance test error under that condition.
The paper does not compare time or training steps to fit true versus completely random labels, nor measure convergence cost as corruption rises.
No experiments use shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The paper reports best-epoch test accuracy across some symmetric-noise rates and training dynamics at selected rates, but does not report perfect training-set fit across the full 0-to-100% corruption range or establish that signal is captured while noise is memorized.

Tests a representation regularizer and fixed versus unfixed encoders under label noise. Does not test whether weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation fail to prevent fitting completely random labels, or whether removing them alone harms true-label generalization.
The clean-first observation is attributed to Arpit et al. (2017); this paper does not independently measure learning order for real versus random labels.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.operation_detail: Train with CE on CIFAR-10 at symmetric label noise rate 0.6, comparing fixed and unfixed SimCLR-pretrained encoders; test accuracy is reported by epoch.
rows.baseline: CE with unfixed encoder; figure only
rows.value: CE with fixed encoder; figure only
rows.note: Text says the fixed encoder is more stable during learning. The plot supplies no tabulated values.
rows.check: Test accuracy over epochs at one corruption rate measures encoder-treatment stability, not degradation across corruption rates or perfect training fit.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.operation_detail: Train with CE at symmetric noise rates 0.2 and 0.4, comparing a representation regularizer with CE alone from SimCLR initialization; test accuracy is plotted by epoch.
rows.note: For the pre-trained encoder, authors say performance gradually decreases without the regularizer and the regularizer can help it gradually increase. Plots provide no exact values.
rows.check: The extracted finding is the proposed regularizer's effect on test accuracy during training. It measures neither training-label fit nor separate clean/noisy-label learning.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.operation_detail: Train with CE at symmetric noise rates 0.4 and 0.6, comparing a representation regularizer with CE alone from random initialization; test accuracy is plotted by epoch.
rows.note: Authors say CE first increases then decreases as training proceeds, while regularized performance is more stable after its peak; at 60% noise, the peak is much higher. No exact values are supplied.
rows.check: Peak-then-decline test accuracy and its mitigation do not directly measure the learning order of clean and noisy training labels or V4's corruption-rate relationship.
